title: Inside 847 Production Clinical AI Notes — Sebastian Fox, Composo
talk_summary: A medical doctor turned eval engineer shows that production clinical-note LLMs fail mostly by quiet omission/over-inference, and that even strong LLM judges with detailed rubrics miss ~1 in 5 serious errors because 'taste' (what matters in context) can't be pre-written. He proposes a discover→capture→calibrate loop: mine real failure modes from production outputs, have experts leave free-form judgments, and retrieve the most similar past judged cases plus corrections into the judge's context per output.

takeaways.technique: Retrieval-calibrated judge instead of static rubric
takeaways.what_they_do: For each output, the judging agent retrieves the most similar previously-judged cases, expert corrections, and reference docs into its context, assembling a case-specific standard on the fly rather than one frozen rubric.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for each output, you retrieve the ones that bear on it into the judges context, add one and it's live on the next call
takeaways.numbers: Static strong judge: ~1 in 5 clean passes still had a serious error; the retrieval loop 'performing a lot better' on same notes (no precise figure given)

takeaways.technique: Discover failure-mode ontology from real outputs
takeaways.what_they_do: Don't invent test cases on a whiteboard; put the system in production, cluster what actually goes wrong, name the failure modes, and use that ontology to drive what to capture and retrieve.
takeaways.evidence_quote: synthetic test cases only cover the failures you already imagined. The ones that hurt you are often the ones that you didn't

takeaways.technique: Free-form expert comments as raw eval material
takeaways.what_they_do: Have domain experts spend a few focused hours leaving free-form comments (reasoning + corrections, not just scores) on real outputs; that record becomes the retrieval corpus for the judge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: easiest place to start is your experts leaving free-form comments on real outputs

takeaways.technique: Asymmetry of verification: checker focuses on one failure at a time
takeaways.what_they_do: Let the generator be cheap and imperfect; put a checker after it that only has to find the one thing wrong, with more tokens/time and explicit failure modes to hunt, since verification is easier than generation for the easy part.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the checker only has to find the one thing that's wrong and just focus on that task

takeaways.technique: Keep 'taste' as retrievable examples, not weights or prompt
takeaways.what_they_do: Store judgment as past examples/corrections and retrieve per-output rather than fine-tuning or stuffing a giant static rubric; changes are live on the next call and explainable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: They go stale, they can't tell you why and you can't change them without a retrain

takeaways.technique: Continuous discover→capture→calibrate loop as a routine
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the eval loop continuously: new failure modes surface from production, flow back into the ontology and retrieval corpus, sharpening the next judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Evaluation isn't something you have, it's something that you do continuously over time
